We have a classic pursuit/meeting problem. Train 1 leaves city A at 60 km/h toward city B. Train 2 leaves city B (450 km away from A) at 90 km/h toward A, but 30 minutes (0.5 hours) later.

Let me set up coordinates: A at x = 0, B at x = 450 km. Train 1 moves in +x direction at 60 km/h, starting at t = 0. Train 2 moves in −x direction at 90 km/h, starting at t = 0.5 h.

Train 1 position: x₁(t) = 60t.
Train 2 position: x₂(t) = 450 − 90(t − 0.5) for t ≥ 0.5.

Meet when x₁ = x₂:
60t = 450 − 90(t − 0.5)
60t = 450 − 90t + 45
60t + 90t = 495
150t = 495
t = 3.3 h = 3 hours 18 minutes.

Position: x = 60 × 3.3 = 198 km from A.

The user is asking about CUDA graphs — a CUDA feature introduced around CUDA 10 that allows capturing a series of kernel launches (and other CUDA work like memcpys, event records, etc.) into a graph structure, then replaying that graph with a single launch. The question is: why can replaying a graph be faster than launching the same kernels eagerly (i.e., one at a time via cudaLaunchKernel), and what are the costs/tradeoffs?

Let me think through the technical reasons why CUDA graph replay is faster:

1. **CPU-side launch overhead reduction**: The biggest win. Each eager kernel launch involves the CPU going through the CUDA runtime/driver stack: parameter marshaling, validation, driver calls (cuLaunchKernel), command buffer writes to the GPU pushbuffer, etc. This can be several microseconds per launch (typically ~5-10 μs, sometimes more with runtime overhead, argument processing, etc.). For graphs, the entire DAG is submitted with a single call (cudaGraphLaunch), so the per-kernel CPU cost collapses to roughly amortized near-zero. This matters most when kernels are short — if your kernels each run for milliseconds, launch overhead is irrelevant; if they run for 5 μs, launch overhead dominates.
